subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 3! You have met decimals before, but in this unit you will take a large step forward and become truly fluent with them. You will focus on two powerful skills: multiplying and dividing decimals by powers of 10, and rounding numbers to a chosen level of precision. Along the way you will use these skills to estimate and check whether an answer is sensible. These are not dusty classroom exercises – they are the everyday tools of scientists, shopkeepers, engineers and anyone who works with measurements and money.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 7 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Explain what a power of 10 is, including negative powers such as 10⁻¹ = 0.1.
Multiply any decimal by 10, 100, 1000 and beyond by moving the decimal point to the right.
Divide any decimal by powers of 10 by moving the decimal point to the left.
Round decimals to a given number of decimal places.
Round numbers to a given number of significant figures.
Use rounding and powers of 10 to estimate the result of a calculation.
Judge whether an exact answer is reasonable by comparing it with your estimate.
Apply these skills to real problems in measurement, money and science.

concepts.title: Understanding Powers of 10
concepts.explanation:
Everything in this unit rests on powers of 10, so let us start there. A power of 10 is any number you can write as 10 raised to some whole-number power. The positive powers grow quickly:

Do you see the pattern? The exponent tells you exactly how many zeros follow the 1. This simple rule makes mental arithmetic with powers of 10 fast and dependable. Each power is ten times larger than the one before it, so the numbers climb the ladder of place value one rung at a time.

Negative powers of 10 are just as important, because they describe the decimal places. A negative exponent means ‘one over that power’:

10⁻¹ = 1/10 = 0.1 (one decimal place)

10⁻² = 1/100 = 0.01 (two decimal places)

10⁻³ = 1/1000 = 0.001 (three decimal places)

Notice the neat mirror image: the negative exponent tells you how many decimal places the number has, just as the positive exponent told you how many zeros. Positive powers stride off towards the large numbers on the left of the decimal point; negative powers step down towards the tiny numbers on the right.

This is exactly why our number system works so elegantly. Every place in a decimal number is a power of 10. Look at the number 3,456.789 and read each digit's home:

There is one more relationship worth knowing. A positive power and its matching negative power are reciprocals – they multiply together to give 1. For example, 10³ × 10⁻³ = 1000 × 0.001 = 1. More generally, 10ⁿ × 10⁻ⁿ = 1. This is the deep reason why multiplying and dividing by powers of 10 have opposite effects on the decimal point, as you are about to see.
concepts.example: Powers of 10 appear everywhere in science. The speed of light is about 3 × 10⁸ metres per second; the mass of an electron is roughly 9 × 10⁻³¹ kilograms. They also power the metric system you use daily: there are 10³ = 1000 metres in a kilometre and 10⁻³ = 0.001 kilometres in a metre. Once you are comfortable with powers of 10, all these conversions become simple.

concepts.title: Multiplying Decimals by Powers of 10
concepts.explanation:
Here is the golden rule: multiplying by a power of 10 moves the decimal point to the right, and the number of places it moves equals the exponent. Multiplying makes a number bigger, so the digits shift into larger place values.

3.456 × 10 = 34.56 (point moves 1 place right)

3.456 × 100 = 345.6 (point moves 2 places right)

3.456 × 1000 = 3456 (point moves 3 places right)

The digits themselves never change – only the position of the decimal point moves. When the point reaches the end of the number we usually stop writing it, so 3456.0 is simply written 3456.

Sometimes you run out of digits and must add zeros as place holders. Take 5.23 × 1000. You need to move the point three places right, but 5.23 only has two digits after the point. Fill the gap with a zero: 5.23 → 52.3 → 523. → 5230. So 5.23 × 1000 = 5230. The extra zero is not decoration; it keeps every other digit in its correct place.

The rule works even for numbers smaller than 1. For 0.0456 × 100, move the point two places right: 0.0456 → 0.456 → 4.56. The leading zeros simply vanish as the point sweeps past them, giving 4.56.

Why does this work? Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times more, which slides it one place towards the larger values on the left. Rather than move all the digits, we find it neater to hold the digits still and move the decimal point the other way – to the right. When 3.456 becomes 34.56, the 3 has changed from meaning ‘3 ones’ to meaning ‘3 tens’, and the 4 has changed from ‘4 tenths’ to ‘4 ones’. The moving point is a picture of these place-value changes.

This gives you a wonderful mental-maths shortcut. To work out 7.89 × 1000 in your head, just jump the point three places: 7890. No long multiplication needed. This same skill lets you check a calculator quickly – if the screen shows something wildly different, you know to look again.
concepts.example: Real examples are everywhere. To change 3.45 metres into millimetres you multiply by 1000 (there are 1000 mm in a metre): 3.45 × 1000 = 3450 mm. If a cell is 0.025 mm across, its width in micrometres is 0.025 × 1000 = 25 micrometres. And if an investment grows a hundredfold, 23.45 shillings becomes 23.45 × 100 = 2345 shillings.

concepts.title: Dividing Decimals by Powers of 10
concepts.explanation:
Division is the mirror image of multiplication, so the rule flips: dividing by a power of 10 moves the decimal point to the left, again by as many places as the exponent. Dividing makes a number smaller, so the digits shift into smaller place values.

345.6 ÷ 10 = 34.56 (point moves 1 place left)

345.6 ÷ 100 = 3.456 (point moves 2 places left)

345.6 ÷ 1000 = 0.3456 (point moves 3 places left)

Notice what happened in the last line: the point moved past the leftmost digit, so we wrote a zero before the decimal point to keep the notation clear and correct. That leading zero is good manners – it makes the number easy to read and hard to misjudge.

As with multiplying, you sometimes need to add zeros. For 56 ÷ 1000, the point starts (invisibly) after the 6. Move it three places left, filling with zeros: 56. → 5.6 → 0.56 → 0.056. So 56 ÷ 1000 = 0.056. And for a decimal such as 12.34 ÷ 100, move two places left: 12.34 → 1.234 → 0.1234.

The reasoning matches Concept 2 in reverse. Dividing by 10 makes every digit worth ten times less, sliding it one place towards the smaller values on the right. Holding the digits still, we move the decimal point the opposite way – to the left. When 345.6 becomes 34.56, the 3 changes from ‘3 hundreds’ to ‘3 tens’, and so on down the line.

Because multiplying and dividing by powers of 10 are inverse operations, they undo each other. If 3.45 × 100 = 345, then 345 ÷ 100 = 3.45. This gives you a free way to check your work: divide your answer back and see if you return to where you started.
concepts.example: The real-world uses are just as common as before. To turn 2500 millimetres into metres, divide by 1000: 2500 ÷ 1000 = 2.5 m. To express 45,000 metres in kilometres, divide by 1000: 45 km. If you have 2340 cents, the amount in dollars is 2340 ÷ 100 = $23.40. And a score of 45 out of 100 is 45 ÷ 100 = 0.45, which is 45%.

concepts.title: Rounding to Decimal Places
concepts.explanation:
Rounding means replacing a number with a nearby, simpler number that has fewer decimal places. We round because real measurements have limits, and because a long string of decimals is often more precise than is useful. The skill is to choose a sensible level of precision and land on the closest number at that level.

The standard rule is short and always the same. Look at the first digit you are cutting off – the one just to the right of the place you are keeping:

If that digit is 5 or more, round up (increase the last kept digit by 1).

If that digit is less than 5, round down (leave the last kept digit unchanged).

Let us round to one decimal place. To round 5.847 to 1 d.p., keep the tenths digit and look at the hundredths (4). Since 4 < 5, round down: 5.8. To round 9.362 to 1 d.p., look at the hundredths (6). Since 6 ≥ 5, round up: 9.4.

Now two decimal places. To round 7.2456 to 2 d.p., keep the hundredths and look at the thousandths (5). Since 5 ≥ 5, round up: 7.25. Whenever the deciding digit is exactly 5, our rule rounds up, so 3.145 becomes 3.15 and 6.235 becomes 6.24 to 2 d.p.

Sometimes rounding sets off a cascade. Round 2.9967 to 2 d.p. The thousandths digit is 6, so we round up. But 2.99 rounded up is not 2.90 – increasing the hundredths carries over into the tenths and then the ones, giving 3.00. Take care here: 2.99 + 0.01 = 3.00, not 2.100. Work the carry through calmly, one place at a time.

A subtle but important point: a trailing zero after the decimal point is meaningful. If a length rounds to 4.50 to 2 d.p., write it as 4.50, not 4.5, because the final zero tells the reader you have worked to the hundredths place. In money this matters too – we write $7.30, never $7.3.
concepts.example: How much precision should you use? Match it to the context. Money usually uses 2 decimal places (cents). Scientific measurements might use three or more, depending on the instrument. And a calculator that shows 0.7580645… does not mean all those digits are meaningful – reporting a test result as 75.8% is far more sensible than 75.80645%.

concepts.title: Rounding to Significant Figures
concepts.explanation:
Significant figures (s.f.) give a way to say how precise a number is, counting from its first meaningful digit rather than from the decimal point. This is the language scientists and engineers use, because it captures precision no matter how large or small the number is.

First you must be able to spot which digits are significant. The rules are systematic:

All non-zero digits are significant. In 2453, all four digits count.

Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. In 2045, the middle zero counts, so it has 4 s.f.

Leading zeros are NOT significant. In 0.00456, only 4, 5 and 6 count – 3 s.f. The zeros just fix the size.

Trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant. In 3.400, all four digits count, because those zeros show measured precision.

To round to a chosen number of significant figures, count that many digits starting from the first non-zero digit, then apply the ordinary 5-or-more rule to the next digit. Round 0.004567 to 3 s.f.: the three significant figures are 4, 5 and 6; the next digit is 7, so round up to 0.00457.

A few more: 0.09876 to 3 s.f. keeps 9, 8, 7 and looks at 6, rounding up to 0.0988. And 1.235 to 3 s.f. looks at the fourth digit (5) and rounds up to 1.24. When a rounded number could be misread, scientific notation removes all doubt: 2500 to 2 s.f. is written 2.5 × 10³, making it plain that only the 2 and the 5 are significant.
concepts.example: Significant figures protect you from false precision. If you measure a length as 15.7 cm with a millimetre ruler, you have 3 significant figures, and any calculation built on that measurement should not pretend to more. A good habit: when you multiply or divide measurements, round the final answer to match the least precise value you used.

concepts.title: Estimation and Approximation
concepts.explanation: Estimation brings all these skills together. To estimate, you round the numbers in a calculation to simple values, work out the easy sum, and use the result to judge whether an exact answer is sensible. Estimation is the mathematician's early-warning system: it catches the big mistakes, like a misplaced decimal point, before they cause trouble. To estimate 47.8 × 23.2, round both numbers: 50 × 20 = 1000. The exact answer is 1109.36, so 1000 is a good guide. More importantly, the estimate would instantly expose a decimal-point slip, such as an exact answer of 110.936 or 11,093.6, because either would be wildly out of line with the estimate of 1000.
concepts.example: For adding and subtracting, round to a convenient place. To estimate 387 + 456 + 234, round to the nearest hundred: 400 + 500 + 200 = 1100. The true sum, 1077, is close. For division, round to numbers that divide evenly, such as estimating 62 ÷ 19 as 60 ÷ 20 = 3 (the exact answer is about 3.26).

methods.title: How to multiply or divide by a power of 10
steps: Read the power of 10 and count its zeros — that is how many places to move.
Decide the direction: multiply moves the point right, divide moves it left.
Slide the decimal point that many places, keeping the digits in order.
Add zeros as place holders if you run out of digits, and a leading zero if needed.

methods.title: How to round to decimal places
methods.example: Round 9.362 to the nearest tenth (1 d.p.).
steps: Identify how many decimal places you must keep.
Look at the very next digit to the right.
If it is 5 or more, round the last kept digit up; otherwise leave it.
Handle any carry (cascade) and keep meaningful trailing zeros.

methods.title: How to round to significant figures
steps: Count significant figures from the first non-zero digit.
Keep the required number of them.
Look at the next digit and apply the 5-or-more rule.
Use place-holder zeros to keep the number the right size.

methods.title: How to estimate a calculation
methods.example: Estimate 6.8 × 9.2, then say whether an exact answer of 62.56 is reasonable.
steps: Round each number to a simple, convenient value.
Do the easy calculation in your head.
Compare the estimate with the exact answer to check it is the right size.

methods.title: Round to decimal places
steps: Keep the hundredths (9) and look at the next digit, the thousandths (3).
Since 3 < 5, round down — leave the 9 as it is.
Answer: 67.89.

methods.title: A rounding cascade
methods.example: Round 156.4999 to the nearest hundredth (2 d.p.).
steps: Keep the hundredths (9) and look at the thousandths (9).
Since 9 ≥ 5, round up.
Rounding 156.49 up by 0.01 gives 156.50 — the carry ripples from the hundredths into the tenths.
Keep the meaningful zero: 156.50.

workedExamples.title: Multiply by a power of 10
workedExamples.solution: 100 = 10², so move the decimal point 2 places right. 3.7 → 37. → 370. We had to add a zero because we ran out of digits. Answer: 370.

workedExamples.title: Multiply a small decimal
workedExamples.solution: 10,000 = 10⁴, so move the point 4 places right. 0.0089 → 0.089 → 0.89 → 8.9 → 89. The leading zeros disappear as the point sweeps past. Answer: 89.

workedExamples.title: Divide by a power of 10
workedExamples.solution: 1000 = 10³, so move the point 3 places left. 234.5 → 23.45 → 2.345 → 0.2345. We add a leading zero for clarity. Answer: 0.2345.

workedExamples.title: Find the missing exponent
workedExamples.solution: Ask how many places the point must move to turn 2.8 into 28,000. 2.8 → 28 → 280 → 2800 → 28,000 is 4 places right, so n = 4. Check: 2.8 × 10⁴ = 2.8 × 10,000 = 28,000. ✓

workedExamples.title: Round to decimal places
workedExamples.solution: Keep the hundredths (9) and look at the next digit, the thousandths (3). Since 3 < 5, round down — leave the 9 as it is. Answer: 67.89.

workedExamples.title: A rounding cascade
workedExamples.prompt: Round 156.4999 to the nearest hundredth (2 d.p.).
workedExamples.solution: Keep the hundredths (9) and look at the thousandths (9). Since 9 ≥ 5, round up. Rounding 156.49 up by 0.01 gives 156.50 — the carry ripples from the hundredths into the tenths. Keep the meaningful zero: 156.50.

workedExamples.title: Round to significant figures
workedExamples.solution: Count from the first non-zero digit: 4, 5, 6 are the three significant figures. The next digit is 7, so round up. Answer: 0.00457. The leading zeros are not significant; they only show the size.

workedExamples.title: Estimate to check a calculation
workedExamples.prompt: Estimate 6.8 × 9.2, then say whether an exact answer of 62.56 is reasonable.
workedExamples.solution: Round: 6.8 ≈ 7 and 9.2 ≈ 9, so the estimate is 7 × 9 = 63. The exact answer 62.56 is very close to 63, so it is reasonable. ✓ If the answer had been 6.256 or 625.6, the estimate would have warned us of a decimal-point error.

workedExamples.solution: a) 0.08, b) 0.079, c) 0.0787 (the fifth decimal digit is 5, round up).

activities.title: The Decimal Point Slide
activities.materials: a strip of paper, a bold marker, and a small paper clip.
steps: Write a decimal number with its digits well spaced, for example 3 . 4 5 6, leaving room to slide the point.
Clip the paper clip onto the decimal point so it can slide left and right.
Call out ‘times 100!’ and slide the clip two places right; read the new number aloud.
Call out ‘divide by 1000!’ and slide it three places left, adding zeros where needed.
Take turns with a partner or your AI tutor calling out operations and reading the results.

activities.title: Metric Conversion Market
activities.materials: a ruler or tape measure, and household objects to measure.
steps: Measure five objects in centimetres, writing each length as a decimal.
Convert each length to millimetres by multiplying by 10 (move the point one place right).
Convert each length to metres by dividing by 100 (move the point two places left).
Make a small table showing each object in mm, cm and m.
Check one row with a partner or your AI tutor: do all three numbers describe the same length?

activities.title: Rounding Card Game
activities.materials: paper cards, each showing a decimal number such as 5.847, 9.362, 0.0567 or 156.499.
steps: Shuffle the cards and place them face down in a pile.
Turn over a card and roll a die: 1 means round to the nearest whole number, 2 means 1 d.p., 3 means 2 d.p. (re-roll 4, 5, 6).
Round the number yourself, or race a partner or your AI tutor; the first correct answer keeps the card.
Watch for cascade cards like 156.499 – they catch people out!
If playing with others, whoever has the most cards at the end wins.

activities.title: The Estimation Challenge (Family Game or Solo)
activities.materials: a shopping receipt or a list of prices, and paper.
steps: Cover the total on the receipt.
Estimate the total yourself (or with family or your AI tutor) by rounding every price to the nearest whole shilling and adding.
Reveal the real total and compare it with your estimate (or, if playing with others, see whose estimate was closest).
Talk about which prices were hardest to round and why.
Play again with a longer list to see if your estimates get sharper.

activities.title: Powers of 10 Scavenger Hunt
activities.materials: curiosity, and any books, labels or packets around the house.
steps: Hunt for numbers that are very large or very small – on food packets, bottles, or in books.
For each one, write it and estimate the nearest power of 10 (is it about 10², 10³, 10⁻³?).
Order your finds from smallest to largest power of 10.
Share the most surprising number you found with your family.
You will start to notice that powers of 10 are hiding on almost every label and sign around you.

activities.title: Investigation – The Vanishing Zeros
steps: Start with 0.0456 and keep multiplying by 10, writing each result: 0.456, 4.56, 45.6, and so on.
Watch carefully: at what point do the leading zeros disappear?
Now start with 4560 and keep dividing by 10. Where does a leading zero appear?
Write a sentence describing exactly when zeros appear and vanish as the point moves.
Predict what happens to 7.0 when you divide by 10 four times, then test your prediction.

rules.title: Powers of 10 Rule
rules.text: The exponent counts the zeros: 10 to the 3 = 1000 (three zeros). A negative exponent counts decimal places: 10 to the minus 3 = 0.001. 10 to the n times 10 to the minus n = 1 (they are reciprocals).

rules.title: Multiply and Divide by Powers of 10 Rule
rules.text: Multiply / Divide by Powers of 10 Multiply: move the decimal point RIGHT (the number gets bigger). Divide: move the decimal point LEFT (the number gets smaller). Move as many places as the exponent; add zeros to fill any gaps.

rules.title: Rounding Rule
rules.text: Find the place you are keeping, then look at the next digit to its right. 5 or more: round up. Less than 5: round down. Watch for a cascade, and keep meaningful zeros like 4.50.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why 5.23 × 1000 needs a zero added, but 5.234 × 1000 does not.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 5.23 × 1000 needs the point to move 3 places but only has 2 digits after it, so one zero fills the gap (5.23 → 52.3 → 523. → 5230). 5.234 × 1000 already has exactly 3 digits after the point, so the point can move all 3 places with no gap to fill (5.234 → 52.34 → 523.4 → 5234).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Estimation and Approximation.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Estimation brings all these skills together. To estimate, you round the numbers in a calculation to simple values, work out the easy sum, and use the result to judge whether an exact answer is sensible. Estimation is the mathematician's early-warning system: it catches the big mistakes, like a misplaced decimal point, before they cause trouble. To estimate 47.8 × 23.2, round both numbers: 50 × 20 = 1000. The exact answer is 1109.36, so 1000 is a good guide. More importantly, the estimate would instantly expose a decimal-point slip, such as an exact answer of 110.936 or 11,093.6, because either would be wildly out of line with the estimate of 1000.

selfAssessment: I can explain what a power of 10 is, including negative powers such as 10⁻¹ = 0.1.
I can multiply any decimal by 10, 100, 1000 and beyond by moving the decimal point to the right.
I can divide any decimal by powers of 10 by moving the decimal point to the left.
I can round decimals to a given number of decimal places.
I can round numbers to a given number of significant figures.
I can use rounding and powers of 10 to estimate the result of a calculation.
I can judge whether an exact answer is reasonable by comparing it with your estimate.
I can apply these skills to real problems in measurement, money and science.
